title: Chipping Away at Chinese AI Risks
gist: A cyber-policy newsletter arguing that the real US-China AI battle is fought over hardware access rather than models: chip export controls are demonstrably biting inside Chinese labs, the proposed CATSR Act would give frontier labs antitrust safe harbor to jointly counter distillation, and Entity List designations would backfire because U.S. firms increasingly depend on Chinese open-weight models. It also reads Iran's low-damage attack on 30+ Minnesota water systems as deliberately calibrated to generate headlines without triggering rally-round-the-flag unity.

insights.claim: The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act proposes safe harbor provisions letting AI companies share information on AI-specific security risks, because without it such sharing could fall afoul of antitrust legislation prohibiting collusion.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
entities: Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act
insights.so_what: Antitrust exemption is emerging as the standard legislative unlock for AI industry coordination — the same mechanism proposed for AI self-regulatory bodies.
insights.locator: The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act

insights.claim: Frontier labs can already detect distillation of their models — evidenced by their repeated after-the-fact complaints — so the value of information-sharing legislation is speed of response and disruption of ongoing campaigns rather than detection capability.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframes the IP-theft problem as a latency problem, which means the fix is operational coordination rather than new detection technology.
insights.quote: We know the frontier labs can already detect distillation because they're always complaining about it after the fact.
insights.locator: The idea here is to encourage frontier labs

insights.claim: Adding Chinese AI companies to the Entity List would likely benefit American frontier AI companies but be a net negative for the broader U.S. economy, because American firms increasingly use open-weight models — the best of which come from the same Chinese labs running distillation campaigns.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A direct conflict of interest between frontier labs and their downstream enterprise customers — expect lab lobbying for sanctions and industry lobbying against.
insights.locator: So, the consensus seems to be that punitive action

insights.claim: After Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Entity List designations would be on the table, a tech industry coalition of 76 companies published an open letter supporting the role of open-weight AI models in the technology mix.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A 76-company coalition mobilizing against sanctions on Chinese model providers quantifies how deeply open-weight Chinese models are embedded in U.S. commercial stacks.
insights.quote: Entity List designations will be on the table
insights.locator: Indeed, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a statement

themes.theme: Compute access, not models, is the decisive front

insights.claim: The battle for AI dominance is being fought around hardware access rather than the models themselves, making reinforcement of chip export controls the single most effective way for the U.S. to stay ahead.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Directs attention to semiconductor policy over model policy as the real determinant of AI leadership — and to the equipment and fab supply chain as the choke point.
insights.quote: Really, though, the battle for AI dominance is being fought around hardware access, not the models themselves.
insights.locator: Really, though, the battle for AI dominance

insights.claim: Journalists Lily Ottinger and Kai Williams touring Chinese AI labs in May found that essentially every AI researcher they spoke to complained their company lacked sufficient access to the advanced compute needed to train and run AI models.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Direct field evidence that export controls are binding — the strongest available counter to the argument that they have failed.
insights.quote: Basically every AI researcher we talked to in China brought up the same complaint: their companies lack sufficient access to the advanced compute resources necessary to train and run AI models.
insights.locator: When AI-focused journalists Lily Ottinger and Kai Williams toured Chinese AI labs

insights.claim: American chip export controls are imperfect but they are biting, so the policy conclusion is to reinforce rather than replace them.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Supports continued or tightened restrictions on advanced accelerator exports — a durable headwind for China-exposed semiconductor revenue.
insights.quote: American chip export controls are imperfect, but they're biting, and reinforcing them is the most effective way for the U.S. to stay ahead.
insights.locator: American chip export controls are imperfect

themes.theme: Open-weight hacking capability as US-China common ground

insights.claim: The recently released open-weight Chinese Kimi K3 model is roughly equivalent to U.S. frontier models from about six months earlier, according to a joint U.S./U.K. evaluation.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A six-month lag between Chinese open weights and U.S. closed frontier models sets the effective commoditization clock for frontier capability.
insights.locator: That time could be only a matter of months away

insights.claim: Universally available powerful AI hacking machines are a shared problem neither the U.S. nor Chinese government will accept, creating a genuine cooperation opening on cyber safety even amid AI competition.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Identifies the one AI domain where US-China negotiation is plausible — worth watching as the first venue for any bilateral AI agreement.
insights.locator: In the areas around AI that aren't about staying ahead

insights.claim: Chinese AI regulation today is focused on protecting the Communist Party's information control and censorship apparatus, but Chinese regulators will eventually rein in the release of very capable open-weight models because hacking done with them will make the Party look bad.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Predicts China will voluntarily restrict open-weight releases on regime-legitimacy grounds — which would remove the main source of free frontier-class models.
insights.quote: The party will not like that kind of political risk, so cyber safety regulation is coming.
insights.locator: China already has strict AI regulation

insights.claim: There is a present window for the U.S. government to engage Chinese regulators and shape forthcoming Chinese AI cyber-safety rules to American advantage before Beijing writes them alone.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Standard-setting influence is time-limited; once China codifies its own rules the U.S. loses leverage over global open-model norms.
insights.locator: But right now there is an opportunity

insights.claim: The coherent three-part strategy — antitrust relief for collective anti-distillation work, tighter chip controls, and engagement with Chinese regulators on hacking capabilities — is unlikely to be executed because long-term strategic thinking is not this administration's strength.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Base case is policy drift rather than coordinated strategy — plan around the status quo persisting.
insights.quote: Long-term strategic thinking is not a Trump admin forte, so we'll hope for the best, but prepare for the status quo.
insights.locator: Will this be what happens?

insights.claim: More than 30 Minnesota community water systems were hit by a coordinated cyberattack, with the worst impact in Braham where residents were asked to limit water consumption for a few hours while the city relied on a single water tower, though drinking water remained safe.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: First large-scale multi-utility water-sector incident of this cycle — a template for low-cost disruption of municipal infrastructure.
insights.locator: Iran's Perfectly Calibrated Cyberattack

insights.claim: Security firm Tenable assesses the operational pattern of the Minnesota water attacks as consistent with CyberAv3ngers, a threat actor associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though there is no formal attribution.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Private-sector pattern attribution is running ahead of government attribution, which is where the actionable signal now appears first.
insights.locator: There is no formal attribution of the Minnesota attacks

insights.claim: U.S. federal agencies updated a warning about Iranian state-affiliated cyber actors targeting critical infrastructure, citing incidents since March in which multiple victims across several sectors were compromised and some experienced operational disruption and financial loss.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A months-long campaign already producing operational and financial damage across sectors — the water attacks are the visible surface of a wider effort.
insights.quote: experienced operational disruption and financial loss
insights.locator: The attack came less than a week after U.S. federal government agencies

insights.claim: The low damage from Iran's Minnesota attacks is a feature rather than a failure: they are significant enough to generate headlines and public unease about the point of an unpopular ongoing war, but not lethal or damaging enough to unify Americans against a single enemy.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframes attack severity as a deliberately tuned political variable — expect a sustained drumbeat of nuisance-level infrastructure attacks rather than escalation.
insights.locator: The Minnesota attacks caused minimal impact

insights.claim: Even a war achieving the White House's stated objectives could still result in an enduring increase in Iran's capacity and appetite for cyber mayhem, because cyber operations against the U.S. and Israel offer propaganda victories with very little chance of a kinetic response.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Military success against Iran raises rather than lowers persistent cyber risk to Western infrastructure — a structurally underpriced consequence of the conflict.
insights.quote: result in an enduring increase in Iran's capacity and appetite for cyber mayhem
insights.locator: In March we wrote that even if the war in Iran

themes.theme: AI security tooling becomes a product category

insights.claim: Microsoft announced a security-focused AI model that, coupled with its MDASH harness, is cheaper and better at vulnerability identification and remediation than current frontier models, signaling that AI security tools are becoming a competitive product category rather than a research demo.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A specialized model beating general frontier models on cost and performance for a security task is the template for vertical AI displacing general-purpose APIs.
insights.locator: AI security tools are a thing

insights.claim: Anthropic reported using Claude Mythos Preview to find flaws in two cryptographic systems, including a proposed post-quantum algorithm then under evaluation by NIST, demonstrating AI used preventively to improve standards rather than to attack them.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: AI-assisted cryptanalysis reaching standards-body candidates means post-quantum migration timelines and algorithm selection carry new model-driven risk.
insights.locator: AI works on cryptographic algorithms too

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced U.S. visa restrictions for cybercriminals including sextortionists and operators of cyber-enabled scams, applying in some cases to their family members.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Extending penalties to family members marks an escalation in personal-cost tools against cybercrime networks that indictments alone could not reach.
insights.locator: U.S. visa restrictions for cybercriminals

insights.claim: Former North Korean Reconnaissance General Bureau cyber operatives hacked the Chosun Central Bank and the Foreign Trade Bank for personal enrichment, converting stolen funds into cryptocurrency, laundering them, and converting back into cash in China.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: State-trained crypto laundering expertise is defecting to personal use, and the China cash-out leg remains the operative bottleneck in North Korean crypto flows.
insights.quote: They used the skills the state trained them with to defend the country, and instead robbed the country’s coffers
insights.locator: North Korean Hackers Hack North Korea

insights.claim: Intrusion Truth identified Guangdong Chanming as the apparent developer of RedRelay, also known as ORBWEAVER, an ORB proxy-botnet network used by almost a dozen Chinese APT groups to hide attack origins, with alleged customers including the People's Liberation Army and the Ministry of Public Security.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shared ORB infrastructure across a dozen APT groups means attribution and takedown leverage concentrates on a small number of contractor firms.
insights.locator: New Chinese cyber contractor identified

insights.claim: Threat actors began actively exploiting CVE-2026-16723 in Alibaba's Fastjson — one of the Java ecosystem's most popular JSON libraries — a day after FearsOff disclosed the flaw, enabling unauthenticated remote code execution against any Java project using it as a component.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A one-day gap between disclosure and mass exploitation in a ubiquitous Java dependency is a broad enterprise exposure event.
insights.locator: A JSON RCE bug is about to rock the Java world

insights.claim: A Russian campaign against Zimbra email servers exploited CVE-2025-66376, a stored cross-site scripting bug patched in November but exploited since at least July, loading a tool called Ulej that harvests credentials, session tokens, backup MFA codes, browser-saved passwords, and 90 days of mailbox contents.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Backup MFA code theft shows second-factor recovery mechanisms are now a primary target — patching alone does not remediate compromised accounts.
insights.locator: Western cyber agencies warn of Russian hacks of Zimbra servers
